title: 1974: fired at Buster Brown's dance hall by Ernest Coycault
summary: At Washington and Central his classical cornet was outplayed by Ernest Coycault blowing blues, and Dink Johnson fired him mid-piece.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: What about the instruments that you played at that time?
Oh, cornet.
You played cornet first.
Yeah, cornet. And I started -- now this is going to be funny. You guys will have to edit this and do it differently.
It's okay.
But a fellow by the name of Buster -- not Buster Wilson, but Buster.
Buster Harding?
No. It wasn't Buster Harding. I can't think of -- I'll think of his name after awhile. Buster Brown.
Buster Brown?

Yeah, his name was Buster Brown, and he had a dance hall up there. He had a dance hall at Washington and Central, and I started to playing in there one night, after they found out I could play a cornet, you know. Didn't call it trumpet at that time. It was the cornet. If we called a cornet a trumpet, somebody called you down. So I was playing -- I went up there to play one night and played a pretty good job. I thought I was doing fine, you know. But a fellow walked in there by the name of Ernest Coycal -- Dink -- Ernest -- Ernest Johnson, not Ernest -- not Dink, but Ernest Coycal. And he walked in there, I was blowing up a breeze. Not much on ragtime, because I'd just had too much classic training, because my father had sent me to an Italian who had taught me clarinet, trumpet and also taught me music, and Italians are very strict teachers. Anyhow, I'll never forget this in my life. Ernest came in there and brought in his cornet. He was a very fine looking gentleman. He was real light, real light. He looked like a white man, to be truthful. Hair was straight as could be, he walked in there.
This was a black man.

Yeah, he was a black man. And he walked in there and took out his cornet and took the horn -- funny -- those keys on he was blowing (Unintelligible) -- I don't know what he was doing to it, but I never had to do that, and I played Chattanooga
(Laughter)

all through the piece, and I played all of Victor Herbert's numbers, trumpet solos -- cornet, it wasn't trumpet, it was cornet. Triple-tonguing, double-tonguing, triple-tonguing and all that, I did all of that. Those Italians had taught me how to do that. And you'd be surprised. When he took that thing out, and a fellow by the name of Buster Wilson was playing the piano, and started playing -- oh, Buster, Buster just started playing the blues, you know, just ordinary blues. Well, I played blues, they laughed at my blues that I played. And so Dink was standing there -- not Dink, but Ernest was standing over there with his cornet, and it was called a cornet at that time, it wasn't a trumpet, and at one part of the thing I was playing and something said (Singing) -- and that was Ernest coming in.
With the cornet, too?
With the cornet. And I said, gee whiz, I ain't going to be able to keep this job.
(Laughter)

And Ernest -- a man playing like that, and you know, Dink Johnson turned around to me and said, "You're fired. We don't need you no more." And that was in the middle of a piece. He wasn't playing nothing but the blues. But that shows you how in that time, even then, you had to be very good at what you were doing or else nobody wanted you.
But getting back to the essence of this thing, I had
to keep going back to that -- see, what I say, we've got to keep going back.
That's fine.
I've got to keep running things in.
Well, if anybody has any things to throw in, you know, we'll just keep it moving.
